text:
[calm, conversational] Artificial intelligence just gave disease a ten-year deadline.
Think of the last time a doctor sat down with someone you love and said a word like cancer.
Or Alzheimer's. Heart disease. Depression.
Now picture your grandkids hearing those words the way you hear the word plague. Something from a history book.
So which of these could really be history by the deadline?
The machines can find cures faster. They can't rush the human body.

Every cure has two dates. The day it's found. And the day it's proven.
And for each of these diseases, the body gives its answer at its own speed. The fastest, in weeks. The slowest, only after decades.

That deadline comes from Dario Amodei. In his words:
"Cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness, these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade."
He runs Anthropic, among the biggest artificial intelligence labs, and he said it in the video made to sell its shares.
This isn't about whether to buy the stock.
He didn't invent it for investors. Years ago, he wrote the same bet into an essay called Machines of Loving Grace. With small print.

And his reasoning is better than it sounds. Trials are slow, he argues, largely because most drugs barely work.
When something works really well, the proof comes fast.
Earlier this year, on a podcast, he made the same point, and set his own limit.

So even in his view, proof takes time.
Less than a decade: that's by twenty thirty-six. Four diseases, and one question for each. When a medicine really works, how fast does the body say so?
The fastest clear answer comes from cancer.

[curious] In the lab, the day a cure is found is already getting closer.
Doctors can rebuild a patient's own immune cells to hunt cancer, with a receptor that works like a hook.
Artificial intelligence now helps redesign those hooks. One new design already works better.
All still in the lab.
Then the body answers. And a tumor answers fast: on a scan, within weeks, it shrinks or it doesn't.
That's how one pill won approval with just fifty-five patients, spread across many different cancers. Most of them responded.

But cancer isn't one disease. It's more than a hundred, and they fight back.
His own essay said so: the end of most cancer, not all. Some rare, difficult cancers may persist.
The line in the sales video just says: cancer.
So cancer, by the deadline: for many kinds, the proof can come in time. Not for every kind.
But is a fast answer always the whole answer?

[thoughtful] Heart disease answers twice.
First, the blood. In a recent trial, people got a single infusion that switched off a gene in the liver.
At the highest dose, weeks later, their bad cholesterol was cut roughly in half.
One treatment, meant to last a lifetime.
But a change to your DNA is for life. So regulators ask to follow patients for up to fifteen years.
And whether the heart attacks really stay away takes a stadium full of people, followed for years.
So heart disease, by the deadline: only halfway. The tool can be ready in time. The proof that it's safe for a lifetime can't.

[warm] This channel exists for one reason: so that the arrival of superintelligence goes well for everybody. In the lab, and at the hospital bed, for your parents, and one day for you. Want that too? Then subscribe.

[thoughtful] The third disease answers fast. The problem is hearing the answer.
Take depression, one part of mental illness. A trial runs for weeks. But in those weeks, many people improve on a sugar pill too.
Even for the antidepressants already approved, only about half the trials beat the sugar pill.
And there's no blood test for depression. The diagnosis is a questionnaire.
That doesn't make it hopeless. In his essay, he wrote that most mental illness can probably be cured.

So mental illness, by the deadline: an open question. Cancer has its scan. The mind is still waiting for one.
And then the fourth disease. The slowest. It starts long before it shows.

Alzheimer's.
The changes in the brain start around twenty years before the first forgotten name.
That means many people who'll be diagnosed by the deadline already carry the first traces today.
So the medicine has to come before the symptoms. Proving that means following healthy people for years, and counting who doesn't get sick.
One such trial waited years for its answer. The drug didn't work.
And for those already sick, his essay had more small print: existing damage may be very difficult to reverse.

The line in the sales video doesn't mention that either.
So Alzheimer's, by the deadline: no. For many who'll get it by then, it has already begun.
[pause] But the race doesn't start at the deadline. It starts now. Since last year, a blood test can spot the first traces.
So if the machines aren't the slow part, why set a date at all?

Partly, because a sales pitch rewards a promise with a date on it. No villain needed.
The Nobel Prize-winning biologist Venki Ramakrishnan, asked in a recent interview about artificial intelligence and new drugs, named the slow part:

The testing, not the finding.
The other reason for Amodei's date: he's betting that the testing can speed up too.
The cardiologist Eric Topol, a fan of what artificial intelligence can do for health, called such cure timelines wildly off-base.
To be fair, Amodei holds himself to a harder test. In August, he wrote that the only thing that will convince people is actually curing cancer.

His own company now designs medicines. One, for muscular dystrophy, went from idea to promising results in mice in under eighteen months.
Its human trials could start as soon as late twenty twenty-eight. Same road as everyone else. First date: fast. Second date: years away.
He even warned of a jam himself, earlier this year, on that same podcast.

Discovery speeds up. Proof jams.
So can proof come sooner, without making medicine less safe?

It can. And it's already starting.
Picture someone you love, around sixty, sharp as ever. At a study clinic, a blood test finds the first traces, years early.
So they join a trial: can a medicine hold off the first forgotten name?
For now, experts advise that test for healthy people only in trials. But that's how the slowest proof gets a head start.
In other trials, part of the sugar-pill group is replaced by a prediction: a digital twin of each patient.

Fewer people on a sugar pill, answers sooner. Europe's regulator accepts it for some trials. It shrinks the comparison group. It doesn't replace it.
At America's regulator, reviewers now work with an artificial intelligence assistant. For a few priority medicines, the goal is a decision within one or two months.
Amodei's own proposal: rules made for medicines that clearly work and are clearly safe. But remember the heart: fast can't mean less safe.

In the sales video, his promise came with a condition. In his words:
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles."
If the machines make the first date come fast, the second date becomes the real deadline. And people set that one.
Clinics that find disease early. Scientists who design leaner trials. Lawmakers who keep the rules in step with medicines that clearly work.
That's what doing it right looks like.

So, does the deadline hold?
Cancer: for many kinds, yes. Heart disease: halfway. Mental illness: still open. Alzheimer's: not by then. But its race has already begun.
[pause] Maybe your grandkids will hear the word Alzheimer's the way you hear the word plague. Not because someone set a date. Because someone proved it.
Every cure has two dates: the day it's found, and the day it's proven.
Investors are already putting a price on the first date. The second one is still ours to move.

[warm] This channel exists for one reason: so that the arrival of superintelligence goes well for everybody. Fast discoveries in the lab, and proof that arrives in time, for every family in a waiting room today. Including yours. Want that too? Then subscribe.
